messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Leila is a 21-year-old Middle Eastern American woman who came to treatment several months after leaving military service, speaking about the deployment in a flat, careful way that suggested how much effort it took to stay composed. She described one night in particular that still stood apart from the rest of her time overseas: a sudden attack after dark, when the base had dropped into that tense half-silence she used to think of as the most dangerous hour. She remembered the jolt of movement, the confusion of running, the sense that her body had been pushed past what it could safely hold. What stayed with her was not a single visual image so much as the bodily memory of strain and exposure in the dark, the feeling that once night came and she had to move fast, she was no longer in control of what could happen.

Since returning home, Leila has built her life to keep that feeling from being stirred up. She now works as a database administrator, a job she chose in part because it lets her sit in a predictable, climate-controlled office and spend most of the day behind a screen. She avoids situations that put her body under stress. She does not exercise beyond what feels absolutely necessary, declines invitations that involve hiking or even long walks, and notices herself becoming uneasy if she has to rush for a train or carry something heavy up the stairs. If her heart rate rises or her muscles start to burn, she pulls back quickly, as though her body is approaching a threshold she cannot afford to cross again. To her, physical strain does not feel healthy or invigorating; it feels like the beginning of danger.

Her evenings have become increasingly restricted. Leila leaves work before sunset whenever she can and feels a steady tightening in herself if a database update or server issue threatens to keep her in the office late. When colleagues suggest getting dinner after work, she usually finds an excuse. Walking through the parking garage at dusk, seeing the light flatten and the shadows lengthen, is enough to make her grip her keys and hurry, her attention narrowing to getting inside the car and home with the doors locked. She has stopped going out at night almost entirely. Friends have begun to comment that she disappears after dark, but to Leila this feels less like a choice than a rule she has had to live by: nighttime is when things happen, when visibility drops, when control disappears.

Inside her apartment, she relies on order in a way that has gradually taken over more of her day. She cleans and reorganizes repeatedly, especially after work and before bed. She wipes kitchen counters that are already clean, lines up items on her desk until the edges match exactly, and restacks bathroom supplies if one label is turned the wrong way. The rituals calm her briefly. She describes a sense that if the room is exact, if everything is in its place, she can settle her body for a moment and feel less exposed. On weekends she can spend hours moving between small tasks—laundry folded and refolded, shelves sorted, surfaces cleaned again—not because she believes the apartment is dirty, but because the repetition gives her a fragile sense of control.

These habits have narrowed her life in concrete ways. At work, Leila is dependable and meticulous, but she volunteers for remote troubleshooting rather than any task that might require staying late in the server room or crossing campus after dark. She keeps protein bars at her desk so she can skip walking to crowded food spots, and she has quietly arranged her routines to avoid any unnecessary exertion. Her sister has complained that visiting Leila no longer feels relaxed, because a dropped jacket or dish left in the sink can pull Leila away mid-conversation to straighten and scrub. Leila knows this makes her seem rigid, and she is embarrassed by how much relief she gets from these routines, but she does not know how else to keep herself steady.

By the time she sought help, the structure she had built around herself was starting to feel like a trap. A recent overnight systems failure required her team to rotate evening coverage, and the prospect of being responsible after dark left her panicked and ashamed. She feared that if she could not avoid night, and if her body were forced into stress again, she would lose whatever control she had managed to construct. What she wants most is simple enough to say and hard for her to imagine: to stay in her job, to see people without arranging her whole life around sunset, and to be able to come home without feeling she must clean and organize for hours just to make it through the night.
